title: The Friction is Your Judgment — Armin Ronacher & Cristina Poncela Cubeiro, Earendil
summary: Armin Ronacher and Cristina Poncela argue that agent speed creates review overload, brittle code and fast-growing debt, and recommend agent-legible codebases and deliberate friction.

assertions.quote: because we produce a lot of output very fast, we are tricked into thinking that we're actually being more efficient

verdicts.note: METR found devs believed they were ~20% faster while measured slower; other studies also show self-reports outrunning measured gains.

assertions.quote: these tools are super addictive. You never know if that next prompt is going to be the one that makes your product work

verdicts.note: This describes subjective experience; no controlled data measures compulsive use of coding agents.

assertions.quote: this pull request that looks really daunting and has 5,000 lines of code in it

verdicts.note: The SmartBear/Cisco review study found defect detection drops beyond ~200-400 LOC per session; AI makes large PRs cheap to produce.

assertions.quote: that has led to more and more code reviews being skipped, being rubber stamped.

verdicts.note: Surveys (e.g. Sonar 2026) report many developers don't always check AI code before committing, despite saying they distrust it.

METR 2025: among experienced OSS maintainers, 75% read every line of AI code and all of them modified it before submitting. This contradicts the claim for this high-standards group only. (Narrow setting, so it limits the claim rather than refuting it.)
Minimal-review commits appear in only 2 of 47 sources (grey, no peer-reviewed corroboration), though the cited Fawzy et al. grey-literature review found 36% of practitioners skip quality assurance.

Participants submitted AI-assisted code that they then explained less well, with the median dropping from 100% to 87.5% correct. This is indirect evidence that generated code gets accepted without full comprehension, gathered in a 75-minute lab task rather than real shipping.

assertions.quote: tries to read a config file and if it doesn't read a config file, it loads some defaults.

verdicts.note: Practitioners widely report agents adding defensive fallbacks and swallowed errors to make code run, but there is little systematic measurement of how often this happens.

Mining 302.6k AI-authored commits: broad exception handling is the single most common introduced issue (41,374, 8.5% of all issues; e.g. Claude Code adding a bare 'except: pass'), consistent with the claim, though there is no human-commit baseline to compare against.

assertions.quote: you're very quickly creating a code base of the size and complexity that the agent itself can no longer dig itself out from.

verdicts.note: Consistent with long-horizon benchmarks such as SlopCodeBench and with studies of AI-code churn and duplication. Evidence is early but points the same way.

assertions.quote: It's creating code in a new file that has already done somewhere else.

verdicts.note: GitClear's 2024-25 analyses found rising duplicated code and falling refactoring with AI adoption.

assertions.quote: for libraries, they tend to excel a lot more ... products ... it's much harder because there are so many interacting concerns and components.

verdicts.note: This fits evidence that gains shrink with complexity and cross-cutting context, but no study directly compares libraries with products.

assertions.quote: you have to design it in the way so that it is also legible for the agent

verdicts.note: Clear structure and smaller units plausibly help agents (and humans), but controlled evidence on how much restructuring improves agent results is thin.

assertions.quote: most of these we actually achieve with uh linting rules.

verdicts.note: Deterministic checks fire every time and give agents concrete feedback, whereas instruction-file rules compete for attention and are followed inconsistently.

assertions.quote: we don't think that a database migration should ever go in without a human making a judgment call on this

verdicts.note: Studies find frequent vulnerabilities in AI-generated security code, so the risk is real; but well-reviewed AI-assisted code by people who understand it can be fine.

assertions.quote: we're producing months and months of technical debt in the in the in the time of weeks, in the time of days sometimes.

verdicts.note: Unreviewed, fast AI output does accumulate debt (GitClear duplication, churn), but debt depends on review discipline, not on whether AI was used per se.

assertions.quote: system architecture, creating reliability in the system, they are not just very good at.

verdicts.note: Humans still own constraints and tradeoffs, but models can now propose reasonable designs when given context; the gap is narrowing.
